notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Pesticides are substances used to prevent, destroy, repel or control pests.
  • Pests include insects, weeds, fungi, rodents, mites, nematodes and other organisms that damage crops or stored products.
  • Pesticides may be chemical, biological or naturally derived.
  • They are used in agriculture, public health, households and storage systems.
  • Improper pesticide use can harm humans, beneficial organisms and the environment.
  • Pesticides should be used only at recommended dose, time and method.
  • Integrated Pest Management aims to minimise unnecessary pesticide use.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pesticide → General Term for Pest-Control Chemicals/Agents

2. Major Types of Pesticides

Pesticides are classified according to the target pest.

Important classes include:

  • Insecticides.
  • Herbicides.
  • Fungicides.
  • Rodenticides.
  • Nematicides.
  • Acaricides.
  • Molluscicides.
  • Bactericides.
  • Algicides.
  • Fumigants.
3. Insecticide
  • An insecticide controls insect pests.
  • It may kill adults, larvae, eggs or specific developmental stages.
  • Insecticides are used in agriculture and vector control.
  • Different insecticides act through different biochemical mechanisms.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Insecticide → Insects

4. Herbicide
  • A herbicide controls unwanted plants or weeds.
  • Herbicides may be selective or non-selective.
  • They may act before or after weed emergence.
  • Herbicides reduce crop competition from weeds.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Herbicide → Weeds

5. Fungicide
  • A fungicide controls fungal plant diseases.
  • Fungicides may act on the plant surface or move within plant tissues.
  • They may be preventive or curative in limited stages.
  • Copper compounds and sulfur have long histories as fungicides.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Fungicide → Fungi

6. Rodenticide
  • Rodenticides control rodents such as rats and mice.
  • They are used in agriculture, storage and public-health settings.
  • Many rodenticides are highly toxic to non-target animals.
  • They must be handled and stored carefully.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rodenticide → Rats and Mice

7. Nematicide
  • Nematicides control plant-parasitic nematodes.
  • Nematodes are microscopic roundworms.
  • Root-knot nematodes are important crop pests.
  • Some nematicides are soil-applied.
8. Acaricide
  • Acaricides control mites and ticks.
  • Mites are not insects.
  • They belong to the arachnid group.
  • Some pesticides have both insecticidal and acaricidal action.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Mite → Arachnid, not insect.

9. Molluscicide
  • Molluscicides control molluscs such as snails and slugs.
  • They may be used in crops where snail or slug damage is important.
  • They are also used in some disease-vector control programmes.
10. Bactericide
  • Bactericides control harmful bacteria.
  • Copper-based compounds can have bactericidal activity in plant disease management.
  • Antibiotics are generally not considered routine agricultural pesticides in broad public-health use because of resistance concerns.
11. Fumigant
  • Fumigants are pesticides that act in gaseous form.
  • They penetrate enclosed spaces, soil or stored products.
  • They are used for stored-grain pests and soil treatment.
  • Fumigants can be extremely hazardous to humans.
  • Application requires strict safety controls.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Fumigant → Pest Control through Toxic Gas/Vapour

12. Pest
  • A pest is any organism that causes economic loss, disease or damage to crops, livestock, stored products or human health.
  • An organism may be a pest in one context but harmless in another.
  • Pest status depends on population level and damage.
13. Economic Threshold Level
  • The economic threshold is the pest population level at which control action should begin to prevent economically significant damage.
  • It is used in Integrated Pest Management.
  • Treatment is not always justified merely because a pest is present.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Economic Threshold → When Control Action Becomes Justified

14. Economic Injury Level
  • Economic Injury Level is the lowest pest population density that causes economic loss equal to the cost of control.
  • The economic threshold is usually set below the economic injury level.
  • These concepts reduce unnecessary pesticide spraying.
15. Broad-Spectrum Pesticide
  • Broad-spectrum pesticides affect a wide range of species.
  • They may control several pests at once.
  • They may also harm beneficial insects and natural enemies.
  • Repeated broad-spectrum use can disturb ecological balance.
16. Selective Pesticide
  • Selective pesticides target particular pests or groups.
  • They generally cause less harm to non-target organisms when properly used.
  • Selectivity is desirable in IPM programmes.
17. Contact Pesticide
  • Contact pesticides kill or affect pests when they directly contact the chemical.
  • Thorough spray coverage is often important.
  • They do not necessarily move throughout the plant.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Contact Pesticide → Direct Contact Required

18. Systemic Pesticide
  • Systemic pesticides are absorbed by plants and transported within tissues.
  • Pests feeding on treated plants may ingest the pesticide.
  • Systemic pesticides can protect new growth depending on the compound.
  • Some systemic compounds move mainly upward through xylem.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Systemic → Absorbed and Transported within Plant

19. Stomach Poison
  • A stomach poison acts when a pest ingests the pesticide.
  • It is especially effective against chewing insects.
  • The pesticide must be present on or within the food source.
20. Repellent
  • Repellents do not necessarily kill pests.
  • They discourage pests from approaching, landing or feeding.
  • Mosquito repellents are common examples.
21. Attractant
  • Attractants lure pests toward traps or toxic baits.
  • Pheromones can be used as attractants.
  • Attractants are important in monitoring and mass trapping.
22. Pheromone
  • A pheromone is a chemical signal used for communication between members of the same species.
  • Sex pheromones are widely used in insect traps.
  • Pheromone traps can monitor pest populations.
  • They can also reduce mating success through mating-disruption strategies.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pheromone Trap → Species-Specific Pest Monitoring

23. Insect Growth Regulator
  • Insect growth regulators interfere with insect development.
  • They can disrupt moulting, metamorphosis or reproduction.
  • They are generally more selective than many older broad-spectrum insecticides.
24. Chemical Classification of Insecticides

Major traditional groups include:

  • Organochlorines.
  • Organophosphates.
  • Carbamates.
  • Pyrethroids.
  • Neonicotinoids.
  • Botanical insecticides.
  • Microbial insecticides.
25. Organochlorine Insecticides
  • Organochlorines contain chlorine in stable organic molecules.
  • Many are persistent in the environment.
  • Some accumulate in fatty tissues.
  • DDT is the best-known example.
  • Many older organochlorines have been banned or severely restricted.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Organochlorine → Persistent + Bioaccumulative

26. DDT
  • DDT stands for Dichloro-Diphenyl-Trichloroethane.
  • It is an organochlorine insecticide.
  • It is highly persistent.
  • It accumulates in organisms and food chains.
  • It was widely used against agricultural pests and disease vectors.
  • Environmental concerns led to severe restrictions in many countries.
📌 Must-Memorise

DDT → Organochlorine → Persistent

27. DDT Discovery and Paul Müller
  • Paul Hermann Müller discovered the insecticidal properties of DDT in 1939.
  • He received the 1948 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
  • DDT became widely used for vector control after its insecticidal properties were recognised.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Paul Müller → DDT Insecticidal Property → Nobel 1948

28. Rachel Carson
  • Rachel Carson wrote Silent Spring.
  • Silent Spring was published in 1962.
  • The book highlighted ecological effects of indiscriminate pesticide use, especially persistent chemicals such as DDT.
  • It became influential in the modern environmental movement.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rachel Carson → Silent Spring → 1962

29. Biomagnification
  • Biomagnification is the increase in concentration of a persistent pollutant at successive trophic levels.
  • DDT is a classic example.
  • Top predators can accumulate much higher concentrations than organisms lower in the food chain.
  • Biomagnification is especially important for persistent fat-soluble chemicals.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Biomagnification → Concentration Increases Up Food Chain

30. Bioaccumulation
  • Bioaccumulation is the buildup of a substance within an individual organism over time.
  • Uptake can exceed elimination.
  • Bioaccumulation can occur even before considering food-chain effects.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Bioaccumulation → Within one organism.

Biomagnification → Across trophic levels.

31. DDT and Birds
  • DDT metabolites such as DDE were associated with eggshell thinning in some birds of prey.
  • Thinner eggshells reduced reproductive success.
  • This became a major example of pesticide effects on non-target wildlife.
32. Organophosphate Insecticides
  • Organophosphates are generally less persistent than organochlorines.
  • Many inhibit the enzyme acetylcholinesterase.
  • This causes accumulation of acetylcholine at nerve synapses.
  • Acute poisoning can cause serious neurological symptoms.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Organophosphates → Acetylcholinesterase Inhibition

33. Examples of Organophosphates

Examples include:

  • Malathion.
  • Chlorpyrifos.
  • Parathion.
  • Diazinon.
  • Toxicity differs widely among compounds.
34. Malathion
  • Malathion is an organophosphate insecticide.
  • It has been used in agriculture and mosquito-control programmes.
  • It inhibits acetylcholinesterase.
  • It is less persistent than DDT.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Malathion → Organophosphate

35. Parathion
  • Parathion is a highly toxic organophosphate insecticide.
  • Its use has been banned or restricted in many places because of acute toxicity.
  • It inhibits acetylcholinesterase.
36. Carbamate Insecticides
  • Carbamates also inhibit acetylcholinesterase.
  • Their inhibition is usually reversible compared with the more persistent enzyme effects of many organophosphates.
  • Carbaryl is a classic example.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Carbamate → Acetylcholinesterase Inhibition

37. Carbaryl
  • Carbaryl is a carbamate insecticide.
  • It has been used against a wide range of insect pests.
  • It can also harm beneficial insects.
38. Pyrethrins
  • Pyrethrins are natural insecticidal compounds obtained from chrysanthemum flowers.
  • They affect insect nervous systems.
  • They break down relatively rapidly in the environment.
  • Natural pyrethrins inspired synthetic pyrethroids.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pyrethrin → Chrysanthemum

39. Pyrethroids
  • Pyrethroids are synthetic chemicals based on natural pyrethrins.
  • They are widely used in agriculture and household insect control.
  • They act mainly on sodium channels in insect nerves.
  • Examples include permethrin, cypermethrin and deltamethrin.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pyrethroid → Synthetic Pyrethrin-Like Insecticide

40. Neonicotinoids
  • Neonicotinoids act on nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in insects.
  • They are often systemic.
  • Examples include imidacloprid and thiamethoxam.
  • Some compounds have raised concerns regarding effects on pollinators.
41. Botanical Pesticide
  • Botanical pesticides are derived from plants.
  • Neem-based pesticides are important examples.
  • Pyrethrins are another botanical insecticide group.
  • Botanical does not automatically mean completely harmless.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Natural pesticide ≠ Always non-toxic.

42. Neem
  • Neem is scientifically known as Azadirachta indica.
  • Neem contains several biologically active compounds.
  • Azadirachtin is an important insecticidal compound.
  • Neem products can act as antifeedants, repellents and growth regulators.
📌 Must-Memorise

Neem → Azadirachtin

43. Azadirachtin
  • Azadirachtin interferes with insect feeding and development.
  • It can disrupt moulting and growth.
  • It has relatively low persistence compared with many conventional pesticides.
  • Neem-based products are commonly used in IPM.
44. Microbial Pesticides
  • Microbial pesticides use microorganisms or their products to control pests.
  • Bacteria, fungi and viruses may be used.
  • They are often species-specific or target-specific.
  • Bacillus thuringiensis is an important example.
45. Bacillus thuringiensis
  • Bacillus thuringiensis is abbreviated Bt.
  • It is a soil bacterium.
  • Certain Bt strains produce insecticidal proteins.
  • These proteins are toxic to particular insect larvae.
  • Bt formulations are used as biological insecticides.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bt → Bacillus thuringiensis → Biological Insecticide

46. Bt Toxin
  • Bt produces crystalline proteins called Cry proteins in many strains.
  • Specific Cry proteins affect specific insect groups.
  • In susceptible larvae, the activated toxin damages the gut.
  • Target specificity is an important feature.
47. Bt Crops
  • Bt crops contain genes from Bacillus thuringiensis that enable production of specific insecticidal proteins.
  • Bt cotton is designed mainly against certain bollworm pests.
  • Bt crops do not make plants resistant to all insects.
  • Resistance-management strategies are important.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Bt crop → Specific insect resistance, not resistance to every pest.

48. Bt Cotton in India
  • Bt cotton was the first genetically modified crop approved for commercial cultivation in India.
  • It was approved in 2002.
  • It was introduced primarily for bollworm control.
  • It does not eliminate the need for all other pest-management practices.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

India's First Commercial GM Crop → Bt Cotton → 2002

49. Nuclear Polyhedrosis Virus
  • Nuclear Polyhedrosis Virus, or NPV, is used as a biological insect-control agent.
  • It is highly specific to certain insect hosts.
  • NPV is particularly useful against some caterpillar pests.
  • It is considered compatible with many IPM programmes.
50. Entomopathogenic Fungi
  • Entomopathogenic fungi infect and kill insects.
  • Beauveria bassiana is an important example.
  • Metarhizium anisopliae is another example.
  • These organisms are used as biopesticides.
51. Herbicide Classification

Herbicides may be classified as:

  • Selective.
  • Non-selective.
  • Pre-emergence.
  • Post-emergence.
  • Contact.
  • Systemic.
52. Selective Herbicide
  • A selective herbicide controls certain weeds while causing relatively little injury to a crop at recommended rates.
  • 2,4-D is a classic selective herbicide used against broad-leaved weeds in some cereal crops.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

2,4-D → Selective Herbicide

53. 2,4-D
  • 2,4-D stands for 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid.
  • It is a synthetic auxin-type herbicide.
  • It mainly controls broad-leaved weeds.
  • It has been used in cereal crops, lawns and other settings.
54. Non-Selective Herbicide
  • Non-selective herbicides can damage or kill a wide variety of plants.
  • They are used where broad vegetation control is required.
  • Glyphosate is a common systemic non-selective herbicide.
55. Glyphosate
  • Glyphosate is a systemic herbicide.
  • It inhibits an enzyme in the shikimate pathway.
  • The pathway is involved in synthesis of aromatic amino acids in plants and many microorganisms.
  • It is widely used for weed control.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Glyphosate → Systemic Herbicide

56. Paraquat
  • Paraquat is a fast-acting contact herbicide.
  • It causes rapid plant tissue damage.
  • It is highly toxic if ingested.
  • Its use is restricted or banned in some jurisdictions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Paraquat → Contact Herbicide

57. Pre-Emergence Herbicide
  • Pre-emergence herbicides are applied before weeds emerge.
  • They often act on germinating weed seeds or young seedlings.
  • Timing is critical.
58. Post-Emergence Herbicide
  • Post-emergence herbicides are applied after weeds have emerged.
  • They may be selective or non-selective.
  • Spray coverage and growth stage influence effectiveness.
59. Fungicide Classification

Fungicides may be:

  • Contact fungicides.
  • Systemic fungicides.
  • Protective fungicides.
  • Curative fungicides.
  • Many fungicides are most effective when used preventively.
60. Bordeaux Mixture
  • Bordeaux mixture is a traditional fungicide.
  • It contains copper sulfate and lime.
  • It was developed in France in the nineteenth century.
  • It is used against several fungal and bacterial plant diseases.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bordeaux Mixture → CuSO₄ + Lime

61. Copper Sulfate
  • Copper sulfate has formula CuSO₄.
  • Hydrated copper sulfate is blue.
  • Copper compounds have fungicidal and bactericidal action.
  • Excessive copper can accumulate in soil.
62. Sulfur as Fungicide
  • Elemental sulfur is one of the oldest fungicides.
  • It is used against powdery mildew and some mites.
  • Its performance depends on temperature and application conditions.
63. Mancozeb
  • Mancozeb is a broad-spectrum contact fungicide.
  • It is used protectively against several fungal diseases.
  • It belongs to the dithiocarbamate group.
64. Carbendazim
  • Carbendazim is a systemic fungicide.
  • It belongs to the benzimidazole group.
  • It inhibits fungal cell division.
  • Resistance can develop with repeated use.
65. Rodenticides — Anticoagulants
  • Many rodenticides act by interfering with vitamin K-dependent blood clotting.
  • Warfarin is an early anticoagulant rodenticide.
  • Second-generation anticoagulants can be more persistent and toxic.
66. Zinc Phosphide
  • Zinc phosphide is a rodenticide.
  • In the acidic stomach, it can release toxic phosphine gas.
  • It is highly hazardous and must be handled carefully.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Zinc Phosphide → Rodenticide

67. Aluminium Phosphide
  • Aluminium phosphide is widely used as a fumigant for stored grains.
  • It releases phosphine gas when exposed to moisture.
  • Phosphine is highly toxic.
  • Aluminium phosphide must be used only by trained personnel under regulated conditions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Aluminium Phosphide → Stored-Grain Fumigant → Phosphine

68. Stored-Grain Pest Control

Methods include:

  • Cleaning storage structures.
  • Drying grain properly.
  • Hermetic storage.
  • Temperature control.
  • Biological and physical methods.
  • Fumigation where legally permitted.
69. Pesticide Formulations

Pesticides are sold in formulations such as:

  • Wettable powders.
  • Emulsifiable concentrates.
  • Suspension concentrates.
  • Granules.
  • Dusts.
  • Soluble concentrates.
  • Baits.
  • Formulation affects handling and application.
70. Active Ingredient
  • The active ingredient is the chemical or biological component responsible for pesticidal action.
  • Commercial products also contain solvents, carriers, surfactants or stabilisers.
  • Label concentration refers to the amount of active ingredient in the formulation.
71. Adjuvant
  • An adjuvant improves pesticide application or performance.
  • Surfactants can improve spreading and wetting.
  • Stickers help pesticide remain on plant surfaces.
  • Drift-control agents can reduce formation of fine droplets.
72. Pesticide Residue
  • Pesticide residue is the amount of pesticide or its relevant breakdown products remaining on food, feed or the environment after application.
  • Residues depend on dose, timing, weather and chemical persistence.
  • Food-safety regulations set permissible residue limits.
73. Maximum Residue Limit
  • MRL stands for Maximum Residue Limit.
  • It is the legally permitted maximum concentration of a pesticide residue in or on a food or agricultural commodity.
  • MRLs are based on approved use patterns and safety assessments.
  • MRL is not simply the dose applied to a crop.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

MRL → Maximum Residue Limit

74. Pre-Harvest Interval
  • PHI stands for Pre-Harvest Interval.
  • It is the minimum time required between the last pesticide application and harvest.
  • It allows residues to decline toward permitted levels.
  • PHI differs among pesticides and crops.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

PHI → Spray-to-Harvest Waiting Period

75. Re-Entry Interval
  • Re-entry interval is the minimum time before workers should enter a treated area without specified protective measures.
  • It reduces occupational exposure.
  • The interval depends on the pesticide and label.
76. Persistence
  • Persistence is how long a pesticide remains active in the environment.
  • Persistent pesticides may provide long control.
  • They also create greater risk of accumulation and long-term ecological exposure.
  • DDT is highly persistent.
77. Biodegradable Pesticide
  • Biodegradable pesticides are broken down more readily by microorganisms or natural processes.
  • Rapid degradation can reduce persistence.
  • Breakdown products must also be evaluated for toxicity.
78. Pesticide Resistance
  • Pesticide resistance is inherited ability of a pest population to survive a dose that previously controlled it.
  • Repeated use of the same mode of action strongly selects resistant individuals.
  • Resistance can occur in insects, weeds, fungi and rodents.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Repeated Same Pesticide → Resistance Selection

79. How Resistance Develops
  • A pest population contains natural genetic variation.
  • Pesticide kills susceptible individuals.
  • Resistant survivors reproduce.
  • Resistance alleles increase in frequency.
  • Repeated selection makes the pesticide less effective.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pesticide Resistance → Natural Selection

80. Preventing Resistance

Important measures include:

  • Rotate pesticides with different modes of action.
  • Avoid unnecessary applications.
  • Use recommended dose.
  • Use biological control.
  • Maintain refuges where required for Bt crops.
  • Integrate non-chemical methods.
81. Pest Resurgence
  • Pest resurgence is rapid increase of a pest after pesticide treatment.
  • It can occur when natural enemies are killed more strongly than the pest.
  • Surviving pests can then reproduce with less biological control.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pest Resurgence → Natural Enemies Destroyed

82. Secondary Pest Outbreak
  • A normally minor pest may become important after pesticide treatment.
  • This can happen when its predators or competitors are eliminated.
  • Broad-spectrum pesticides can contribute to secondary pest outbreaks.
83. Non-Target Organisms

Pesticides can harm:

  • Pollinators.
  • Predators.
  • Parasitoids.
  • Earthworms.
  • Fish.
  • Birds.
  • Soil microorganisms.
  • Humans.
  • Selective application helps reduce non-target effects.
84. Pollinators
  • Bees are important crop pollinators.
  • Pesticides applied during flowering can expose bees.
  • Spray timing and pesticide selection are important for pollinator safety.
  • Avoiding unnecessary spraying during peak bee activity reduces risk.
85. Natural Enemies

Important natural enemies include:

  • Predatory insects.
  • Spiders.
  • Parasitoid wasps.
  • Pathogenic microorganisms.
  • Conserving natural enemies reduces pest populations naturally.
86. Ladybird Beetle
  • Ladybird beetles are predators of aphids and other soft-bodied insects.
  • They are beneficial insects.
  • Broad-spectrum insecticides can kill them.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ladybird Beetle → Beneficial Predator

87. Trichogramma
  • Trichogramma are tiny parasitoid wasps.
  • They parasitise eggs of many moth pests.
  • They are widely used in biological pest control.
  • They are released in several agricultural crops.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Trichogramma → Egg Parasitoid

88. Biological Control
  • Biological control uses living organisms to suppress pests.
  • Natural enemies include predators, parasitoids and pathogens.
  • Biological control reduces dependence on chemical pesticides.
  • It is an important component of IPM.
89. Classical Biological Control
  • Classical biological control introduces a natural enemy from the pest's original region.
  • The aim is long-term establishment and control.
  • It requires careful ecological assessment to avoid unintended effects.
90. Conservation Biological Control
  • Conservation biological control protects and encourages natural enemies already present.
  • Reduced broad-spectrum pesticide use helps.
  • Flowering refuges can provide food for beneficial insects.
91. Mechanical Pest Control

Examples include:

  • Hand picking.
  • Trapping.
  • Tillage.
  • Removal of infected plant parts.
  • Barriers and nets.
  • Mechanical methods avoid chemical residues.
92. Physical Pest Control

Examples include:

  • Heat treatment.
  • Cold treatment.
  • Solarisation.
  • Light traps.
  • Sticky traps.
  • Controlled atmosphere.
93. Light Trap
  • Light traps attract nocturnal insects.
  • They are useful for monitoring and sometimes mass trapping.
  • They may also attract non-target insects.
94. Yellow Sticky Trap
  • Yellow sticky traps attract many flying insects such as whiteflies and aphids.
  • They are useful for monitoring.
  • Trap colour exploits insect visual responses.
95. Pheromone Trap
  • Pheromone traps are highly species-specific.
  • They are used to monitor moth pests.
  • They can determine the correct time for control measures.
  • Mass trapping can reduce some pest populations.
96. Cultural Pest Control

Cultural practices include:

  • Crop rotation.
  • Timely sowing.
  • Field sanitation.
  • Resistant varieties.
  • Proper irrigation.
  • Balanced fertilization.
  • Destruction of crop residues carrying pests.
97. Crop Rotation and Pest Control
  • Growing different crop families in sequence can break pest life cycles.
  • Rotation is especially useful for soil-borne pests and diseases.
  • It is less effective against highly mobile pests with broad host ranges.
98. Resistant Crop Varieties
  • Crop varieties may possess natural resistance to pests or diseases.
  • Host-plant resistance reduces pesticide requirement.
  • Resistance may be physical, chemical or genetic.
99. Integrated Pest Management
  • IPM stands for Integrated Pest Management.
  • IPM combines biological, cultural, physical, genetic and chemical methods.
  • Chemical pesticides are used only when necessary.
  • Economic thresholds guide interventions.
  • IPM aims for economically acceptable pest control with minimal environmental harm.
📌 Must-Memorise

IPM → Integrated Pest Management

100. IPM Principles

Important principles include:

  • Pest monitoring.
  • Correct pest identification.
  • Economic threshold.
  • Prevention.
  • Biological control.
  • Resistant varieties.
  • Selective pesticides when required.
  • Rotation of modes of action.
101. IPM Does Not Mean Zero Pesticides
  • IPM does not necessarily prohibit chemical pesticides.
  • It aims to use them judiciously.
  • The goal is pest management, not total pest eradication.
  • A small pest population may be economically tolerable.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

IPM ≠ Complete Ban on Pesticides.

102. Integrated Weed Management
  • Integrated Weed Management combines crop competition, tillage, mulching, manual removal and herbicides.
  • Reliance on one herbicide alone promotes resistance.
  • Crop rotation helps manage resistant weeds.
103. Integrated Disease Management
  • Integrated Disease Management combines resistant varieties, sanitation, crop rotation, biological agents and fungicides.
  • Disease forecasting can help determine spray timing.
104. Pesticide Drift
  • Drift is movement of pesticide droplets or vapour away from the intended target.
  • Wind increases spray drift.
  • Very fine droplets drift more easily.
  • Drift can contaminate neighbouring crops, water bodies and homes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Spray Drift → Off-Target Movement

105. Reducing Drift
  • Avoid spraying in strong winds.
  • Use appropriate nozzle and pressure.
  • Use larger droplets where suitable.
  • Maintain buffer zones near sensitive areas.
  • Follow label instructions.
106. Runoff
  • Pesticides can move with rain or irrigation water over the soil surface.
  • Runoff can contaminate ponds, streams and rivers.
  • Vegetative buffer strips can reduce movement.
107. Leaching
  • Leaching is downward movement of pesticide through soil with water.
  • Highly soluble, persistent pesticides pose greater groundwater risk.
  • Soil texture and organic matter affect leaching.
108. Soil Adsorption
  • Some pesticides bind to clay and organic matter.
  • Strongly adsorbed pesticides are less mobile.
  • However, they may persist longer in soil.
  • Soil pH can influence adsorption and degradation.
109. Pesticide Degradation

Pesticides can break down through:

  • Microbial degradation.
  • Photodegradation.
  • Hydrolysis.
  • Oxidation.
  • Reduction.
  • Degradation rate depends on temperature, moisture and soil conditions.
110. Photodegradation
  • Sunlight can break down pesticides on leaves, soil and water surfaces.
  • Ultraviolet radiation is particularly important.
  • Photodegradation reduces persistence of some pesticides.
111. Microbial Degradation
  • Soil microorganisms can metabolise pesticides.
  • Warm, moist, biologically active soils often promote degradation.
  • Some pesticides are degraded slowly if microorganisms cannot use them effectively.
112. Pesticide Half-Life
  • Environmental half-life is the time required for half of a pesticide amount to degrade or dissipate under specified conditions.
  • Half-life varies greatly among pesticides and environments.
  • It is not identical to radioactive half-life.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Pesticide half-life → Chemical/environmental dissipation.

Radioactive half-life → Nuclear decay.

113. Acute Toxicity
  • Acute toxicity results from high exposure over a short period.
  • Symptoms can develop rapidly.
  • Some organophosphates have high acute toxicity.
  • Poisoning requires immediate medical attention.
114. Chronic Toxicity
  • Chronic toxicity results from repeated or prolonged exposure.
  • Effects may develop over months or years.
  • Possible outcomes depend on pesticide and dose.
  • Long-term risks are assessed during pesticide registration.
115. LD50
  • LD₅₀ means median lethal dose.
  • It is the dose expected to kill 50% of a test population under specified conditions.
  • It is often expressed in mg of substance per kg body weight.
  • Lower LD₅₀ generally indicates greater acute toxicity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lower LD₅₀ → Higher Acute Toxicity

116. LC50
  • LC₅₀ means median lethal concentration.
  • It is commonly used for inhalation or aquatic toxicity studies.
  • It is the concentration lethal to 50% of test organisms under specified conditions.
117. Dose Makes the Poison
  • Toxicity depends on dose and exposure.
  • Even naturally occurring substances can be harmful at sufficiently high doses.
  • Hazard and risk are not identical.
118. Hazard vs Risk
  • Hazard is the inherent ability of a substance to cause harm.
  • Risk depends on hazard plus actual exposure.
  • A highly hazardous chemical can have lower risk if exposure is effectively prevented.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Risk = Hazard + Exposure Context

119. Routes of Pesticide Exposure

Major exposure routes are:

  • Skin contact.
  • Inhalation.
  • Ingestion.
  • Eye contact.
  • Skin exposure is common during agricultural handling.
120. Personal Protective Equipment

PPE may include:

  • Gloves.
  • Protective clothing.
  • Boots.
  • Eye protection.
  • Respirators where specified.
  • Face shields.
  • PPE must match the pesticide label and exposure route.
121. Safe Pesticide Handling
  • Read the label before use.
  • Use only recommended dose.
  • Do not mix pesticides unless specifically permitted.
  • Avoid eating or smoking during application.
  • Wash hands and exposed skin after use.
  • Store pesticides away from food, feed and children.
122. Pesticide Label

The pesticide label provides:

  • Active ingredient.
  • Target pests.
  • Approved crops.
  • Dose.
  • Application method.
  • Safety precautions.
  • Pre-harvest interval.
  • First-aid information.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pesticide Label → Legal/Safety Instruction

123. Pesticide Storage
  • Store in original labelled containers.
  • Keep containers tightly closed.
  • Keep them in locked areas.
  • Do not transfer pesticides into food or drink bottles.
  • Keep away from children and animals.
124. Empty Pesticide Containers
  • Empty pesticide containers should not be reused for food, water or household purposes.
  • Disposal should follow approved regulations.
  • Residual pesticide can remain in apparently empty containers.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Never reuse pesticide container for drinking water or food.

125. Pesticide Poisoning

Possible symptoms vary by chemical and may include:

  • Nausea.
  • Vomiting.
  • Excess sweating.
  • Difficulty breathing.
  • Confusion.
  • Muscle twitching.
  • Convulsions in severe poisoning.
  • Emergency medical evaluation is necessary for suspected poisoning.
126. Organophosphate Poisoning
  • Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase.
  • Acetylcholine accumulates.
  • Symptoms may include excessive salivation, sweating, breathing difficulty and muscle weakness.
  • Severe poisoning can be fatal.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Organophosphate Poisoning → Excess Acetylcholine

127. Antidote Link
  • Atropine is an important antidotal medicine used in organophosphate poisoning under medical supervision.
  • Oximes such as pralidoxime may also be used for selected organophosphate poisonings.
  • Treatment requires trained medical care.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Organophosphate Poisoning → Atropine

128. Pesticides and Water Pollution
  • Runoff can carry pesticides into surface water.
  • Leaching can contaminate groundwater.
  • Aquatic organisms may be highly sensitive.
  • Persistent pesticides can accumulate in sediments.
129. Pesticides and Soil
  • Pesticides can alter soil microbial communities.
  • Some may harm earthworms and beneficial organisms.
  • Others degrade rapidly with little long-term effect.
  • Impact depends strongly on chemical and dose.
130. Pesticides and Food Chains
  • Persistent lipophilic pesticides can enter food chains.
  • They can bioaccumulate.
  • Concentrations may biomagnify at higher trophic levels.
  • This is why persistent organic pollutants receive strict regulation.
131. Persistent Organic Pollutants
  • POPs are persistent organic pollutants.
  • They resist environmental degradation.
  • They can travel long distances.
  • Many accumulate in living organisms.
  • Several older pesticides are classified as POPs.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

POP → Persistent + Bioaccumulative + Long-Range Transport

132. Stockholm Convention
  • The Stockholm Convention addresses persistent organic pollutants internationally.
  • It aims to eliminate or restrict production and use of listed POPs.
  • DDT is among chemicals subject to international restriction, with limited disease-vector-control exemptions under specified conditions.
133. Endosulfan
  • Endosulfan is an organochlorine insecticide.
  • It is persistent and toxic.
  • It has been associated with serious environmental and health concerns.
  • Its use has been banned or severely restricted in many countries.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Endosulfan → Organochlorine Insecticide

134. Endosulfan and India
  • Endosulfan became a major environmental and public-health controversy in India.
  • The Supreme Court of India imposed an interim nationwide ban on manufacture, sale and use in 2011.
  • It is also listed for global elimination under the Stockholm Convention, subject to its provisions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Endosulfan Ban in India → 2011

135. Pesticide Residue Washing
  • Washing fruits and vegetables can remove some surface residues.
  • Peeling may reduce some residues.
  • Systemic pesticide residues inside tissues cannot be completely removed by washing.
  • Correct agricultural use remains the primary method of residue control.
136. Organic Farming and Pesticides
  • Organic farming restricts many synthetic pesticides.
  • Certain biological, mineral and botanical pesticides may be allowed.
  • Organic does not mean pesticide-free in every case.
  • Allowed products still require safe use.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Organic farming ≠ Absolutely no pesticide of any kind.

137. Biopesticide
  • Biopesticides are pest-control agents derived from microorganisms, plants or naturally occurring substances.
  • Examples include Bt, neem and NPV.
  • They are generally more target-specific than many conventional pesticides.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Biopesticides → Bt + Neem + NPV

138. Advantages of Biopesticides
  • Often target-specific.
  • Usually lower environmental persistence.
  • Often safer for natural enemies.
  • Compatible with IPM.
  • Reduced chemical-residue concerns in many cases.
139. Limitations of Biopesticides
  • Often act more slowly.
  • May require precise environmental conditions.
  • Shelf life may be shorter.
  • Target range may be narrow.
  • Correct timing is important.
140. Integrated Pest Management Components
  • Monitoring.
  • Economic threshold.
  • Resistant varieties.
  • Crop rotation.
  • Sanitation.
  • Mechanical control.
  • Biological control.
  • Pheromone traps.
  • Biopesticides.
  • Selective chemical pesticides as last or necessary option.
141. Important Pest-Control Agent Pairs
  • DDT → Organochlorine.
  • Malathion → Organophosphate.
  • Carbaryl → Carbamate.
  • Cypermethrin → Pyrethroid.
  • Imidacloprid → Neonicotinoid.
  • Neem → Azadirachtin.
  • Bt → Microbial insecticide.
  • 2,4-D → Selective herbicide.
  • Glyphosate → Systemic herbicide.
  • Paraquat → Contact herbicide.
  • Bordeaux mixture → Fungicide.
  • Zinc phosphide → Rodenticide.
  • Aluminium phosphide → Fumigant.
142. Important Biological-Control Pairs
  • Trichogramma → Egg parasitoid.
  • Ladybird beetle → Aphid predator.
  • Bt → Insect pathogen.
  • NPV → Viral biopesticide.
  • Beauveria → Entomopathogenic fungus.
  • Metarhizium → Entomopathogenic fungus.
143. Important Scientist–Fact Pairs
  • Paul Hermann Müller → DDT insecticidal action.
  • Rachel Carson → Silent Spring.
  • Louis Pasteur and early microbiologists → Foundation of microbial disease understanding, indirectly relevant to biological control.
  • Modern IPM developed from ecological pest-management concepts rather than one single inventor.
144. Important Dates
  • DDT insecticidal property recognised by Müller → 1939.
  • Müller Nobel Prize → 1948.
  • Silent Spring published → 1962.
  • Bt cotton approved commercially in India → 2002.
  • Interim nationwide endosulfan ban by Supreme Court of India → 2011.
145. Must-Memorise Classification
  • Insecticide → Insect.
  • Herbicide → Weed.
  • Fungicide → Fungus.
  • Rodenticide → Rodent.
  • Nematicide → Nematode.
  • Acaricide → Mite/tick.
  • Molluscicide → Snail/slug.
  • Fumigant → Gas-phase pest control.
146. Must-Memorise Environmental Concepts
  • Persistence → Long environmental lifetime.
  • Bioaccumulation → Buildup in organism.
  • Biomagnification → Increase up food chain.
  • Resistance → Genetic survival after repeated use.
  • Resurgence → Pest rebounds after natural enemies are killed.
  • Drift → Spray moves off target.
  • Runoff → Surface-water movement.
  • Leaching → Downward movement through soil.
  • MRL → Maximum Residue Limit.
  • PHI → Pre-Harvest Interval.
147. TNPSC Traps
  • Pesticide is a broad term.
  • Insecticide is only one type of pesticide.
  • Herbicide controls weeds.
  • Fungicide controls fungal diseases.
  • Rodenticide controls rodents.
  • Mites are not insects.
  • DDT is an organochlorine.
  • DDT is persistent and bioaccumulative.
  • Paul Müller is linked with DDT's insecticidal properties.
  • Rachel Carson wrote Silent Spring.
  • Silent Spring was published in 1962.
  • Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase.
  • Carbamates also affect acetylcholinesterase.
  • Pyrethrins come from chrysanthemum.
  • Pyrethroids are synthetic relatives of pyrethrins.
  • Neem's important compound is azadirachtin.
  • Bt stands for Bacillus thuringiensis.
  • Bt is a bacterial biopesticide.
  • Bt cotton does not control every insect pest.
  • Bt cotton was approved in India in 2002.
  • 2,4-D is a selective herbicide.
  • Glyphosate is systemic.
  • Paraquat is contact herbicide.
  • Bordeaux mixture contains copper sulfate and lime.
  • Zinc phosphide is a rodenticide.
  • Aluminium phosphide releases phosphine.
  • Trichogramma is an egg parasitoid.
  • Ladybird beetles are beneficial predators.
  • Pesticide resistance is a natural-selection process.
  • Pest resurgence can occur after killing natural enemies.
  • IPM does not mean zero pesticide use.
  • MRL and PHI are different.
  • Bioaccumulation and biomagnification are different.
  • Lower LD₅₀ means higher acute toxicity.
  • Organic farming is not necessarily pesticide-free.
  • Washing cannot remove all systemic residues.
  • Pesticide containers must never be reused for food or drinking water.
148. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Pesticide → Broad term.
  • Insecticide → Insects.
  • Herbicide → Weeds.
  • Fungicide → Fungi.
  • Rodenticide → Rodents.
  • Nematicide → Nematodes.
  • Acaricide → Mites.
  • DDT → Organochlorine.
  • Malathion → Organophosphate.
  • Carbaryl → Carbamate.
  • Pyrethrin → Chrysanthemum.
  • Neem → Azadirachtin.
  • Bt → Bacillus thuringiensis.
  • 2,4-D → Selective herbicide.
  • Glyphosate → Systemic herbicide.
  • Paraquat → Contact herbicide.
  • Bordeaux → CuSO₄ + Lime.
  • Zinc phosphide → Rodenticide.
  • Aluminium phosphide → Fumigant.
  • Bioaccumulation → One organism.
  • Biomagnification → Food chain.
  • Resistance → Natural selection.
  • IPM → Integrated Pest Management.
  • MRL → Residue limit.
  • PHI → Waiting period to harvest.
  • Lower LD₅₀ → More toxic.
Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • What is a pesticide? → Substance or agent used to prevent, destroy, repel or control pests.
  • Pesticide controlling insects? → Insecticide.
  • Pesticide controlling weeds? → Herbicide.
  • Pesticide controlling fungi? → Fungicide.
  • Pesticide controlling rats and mice? → Rodenticide.
  • Pesticide controlling nematodes? → Nematicide.
  • Pesticide controlling mites and ticks? → Acaricide.
  • Are mites insects? → No, they are arachnids.
  • Pesticide acting in gaseous form? → Fumigant.
  • What is a broad-spectrum pesticide? → One affecting many pest species.
  • What is a selective pesticide? → One designed to affect particular pest groups with less non-target impact.
  • Contact pesticide means? → Pest must contact the pesticide.
  • Systemic pesticide means? → Pesticide is absorbed and transported in plant tissues.
  • What is a pheromone trap used for? → Species-specific pest monitoring/trapping.
  • Economic threshold means? → Pest level at which control action should begin.
  • What does DDT stand for? → Dichloro-Diphenyl-Trichloroethane.
  • DDT belongs to which group? → Organochlorines.
  • Major environmental property of DDT? → Persistence and bioaccumulation.
  • Scientist associated with DDT insecticidal property? → Paul Hermann Müller.
  • Year DDT insecticidal action recognised? → 1939.
  • Müller's Nobel Prize year? → 1948.
  • Who wrote Silent Spring? → Rachel Carson.
  • Silent Spring publication year? → 1962.
  • Bioaccumulation means? → Buildup of chemical within an organism.
  • Biomagnification means? → Increasing concentration at higher trophic levels.
  • Classic pesticide associated with biomagnification? → DDT.
  • Major effect of DDE in birds? → Eggshell thinning.
  • Organophosphates mainly inhibit? → Acetylcholinesterase.
  • Example of organophosphate? → Malathion.
  • Another highly toxic traditional organophosphate? → Parathion.
  • Carbamates act mainly on? → Acetylcholinesterase.
  • Example of carbamate? → Carbaryl.
  • Natural pyrethrins obtained from? → Chrysanthemum flowers.
  • Synthetic relatives of pyrethrins? → Pyrethroids.
  • Examples of pyrethroids? → Cypermethrin, permethrin, deltamethrin.
  • Important neem pesticide compound? → Azadirachtin.
  • Neem scientific name? → Azadirachta indica.
  • Bt stands for? → Bacillus thuringiensis.
  • Bt is what type of organism? → Bacterium.
  • Bt toxin proteins commonly called? → Cry proteins.
  • Bt cotton targets mainly? → Certain bollworm pests.
  • Was Bt cotton India's first commercially approved GM crop? → Yes.
  • Bt cotton approval year in India? → 2002.
  • Biopesticide virus example? → NPV.
  • Biopesticide fungus examples? → Beauveria and Metarhizium.
  • Selective broad-leaf herbicide commonly asked? → 2,4-D.
  • 2,4-D full chemical name? → 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid.
  • Systemic non-selective herbicide? → Glyphosate.
  • Fast contact herbicide? → Paraquat.
  • Traditional fungicide made from copper sulfate and lime? → Bordeaux mixture.
  • Common contact fungicide? → Mancozeb.
  • Systemic fungicide example? → Carbendazim.
  • Rodenticide example? → Zinc phosphide.
  • Stored-grain fumigant? → Aluminium phosphide.
  • Gas released by aluminium phosphide? → Phosphine.
  • Egg parasitoid used in biological control? → Trichogramma.
  • Aphid predator commonly asked? → Ladybird beetle.
  • What is biological control? → Using natural enemies to suppress pests.
  • What is IPM? → Integrated Pest Management.
  • Does IPM ban all pesticide use? → No.
  • Main aim of IPM? → Economically effective pest control with minimal environmental harm.
  • Important IPM methods? → Monitoring, thresholds, biological, cultural, mechanical and selective chemical control.
  • Repeated use of same pesticide can cause? → Resistance.
  • Pesticide resistance develops through? → Natural selection.
  • Pest population rebound after natural enemies are killed? → Pest resurgence.
  • Minor pest becoming major after pesticide use? → Secondary pest outbreak.
  • Movement of spray away from target? → Drift.
  • Movement across soil surface with water? → Runoff.
  • Downward movement through soil? → Leaching.
  • What is MRL? → Maximum Residue Limit.
  • What is PHI? → Pre-Harvest Interval.
  • What does PHI indicate? → Minimum waiting time between final spray and harvest.
  • What is re-entry interval? → Minimum time before safe worker re-entry after treatment.
  • What does LD₅₀ measure? → Median lethal dose.
  • Lower LD₅₀ indicates? → Greater acute toxicity.
  • What does LC₅₀ measure? → Median lethal concentration.
  • Main exposure routes? → Skin, inhalation, ingestion and eyes.
  • Most common occupational pesticide exposure route? → Skin contact.
  • Basic pesticide safety? → Read label, use PPE, correct dose and safe storage.
  • Can empty pesticide bottles be reused for water? → No.
  • What enzyme is inhibited in organophosphate poisoning? → Acetylcholinesterase.
  • Important medical antidote associated with organophosphate poisoning? → Atropine.
  • What are persistent organic pollutants? → Persistent, bioaccumulative organic pollutants capable of long-range environmental transport.
  • International convention on POPs? → Stockholm Convention.
  • Endosulfan belongs to which class? → Organochlorine insecticide.
  • Supreme Court interim nationwide endosulfan ban year in India? → 2011.
  • Can washing remove all pesticide residues? → No, especially not internal systemic residues.
  • Organic farming means no pesticides whatsoever? → No.
  • Examples of biopesticides? → Bt, neem and NPV.
  • Core TNPSC memory line? → DDT → organochlorine; Malathion → organophosphate; Neem → azadirachtin; Bt → bacterial biopesticide; 2,4-D → selective herbicide; Bordeaux mixture → copper sulfate + lime; IPM → integrated control with minimum necessary pesticide use.
